sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Within one screen or image, does each kind of element look the same everywhere it appears?** No. In the first card (about x 70–316, y 293–473), "Window cleaning" uses a dark, warm photo of an ornate panelled room with leather sofas. The other three cards (x 368–1210, same rows) use flat illustrations in teal and orange on a pale mint panel. Those three set the pattern for the row, and the first card breaks it. The photo is the darkest and busiest thing on the page, so it pulls the eye away from the headline and makes "Window cleaning" look like the featured service, though nothing says it is. It also looks like an asset that never got swapped for its illustration, which makes a booking site seem unfinished. The photo doesn't even show cleaning; it shows a lounge. Why: elements of one kind share one style unless the rules call for a variant (Gerstner, *Designing Programmes*, under "Repeated elements follow one program"; Nielsen 4, consistency and standards). Fix: give Window cleaning a flat illustration on the same mint panel, made in the same style as the other three. If photos are the intended direction, use them on all four cards. Defect. Weight: major.
2. *(Not a checklist line. Passed on for the director's copy check.)* The prices "From $89", "From $189", "From $24" and "From $65" (y ≈ 614) say nothing about what they buy. A visitor can't tell whether $24 laundry is per load, per bag or per week, or whether $89 window cleaning is per visit or per window. These are the numbers people will hold the business to. Fix: add the unit, for example "From $24 per bag" or "From $89 per visit". Defect. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- Color and shape carry the mood. The cream background, deep teal-navy, soft coral and rounded shapes feel calm and trustworthy, which suits letting strangers into your home. The serif in the wordmark and headline adds a homely warmth without feeling twee.
- The headline and subhead say what this is straight away. "Pick a service, choose a day, and a vetted crew arrives with their own supplies" names who does what, and when, with nothing for the visitor to fill in.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (each kind of element looks the same everywhere).

**Walk (working notes)**
- First read: the eye lands on the serif headline at the top left (about 56–672 px across, 115–200 px down). It moves next to the dark window photo in card 1, then to the "Book a visit" button. The page reads as a calm, tidy booking page for a local home-services company.
- Job (assumed, since nothing was given): a homeowner should understand the offer, pick a service, and book.
- Crops: the image is one screen, so I worked from the whole image. Bash was refused, so I could not run the crop or entries scripts. Every line came out yes, so no entries were needed.
- One element stands clearly above the rest: **yes**. The headline is about 40 px, bold, dark serif, and nothing else is close in size.
- Each text level is distinct, with no two sizes almost the same: **yes**. The levels are headline (~40 serif bold), intro (~18 regular grey), card titles (~19 bold sans), body (~15 regular) and price (~15 bold green). The intro and card titles are close in size, but they differ in weight and color and never sit next to each other.
- Headings differ from text by more than size: **yes**. The headline has a serif against sans body text, and the card titles are bold against regular body.

---

**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
None of the checklist lines failed. Two smaller things outside the checklist:
1. **The photo in card 1 competes with the headline (not a checklist line).** The window photo (70–316, 293–473 px) is the only photo on the page; the other three cards are flat pastel illustrations. It is also the only area with a full dark-to-light range. After the headline it is the strongest pull on the page, so "Window cleaning" looks like the featured service when nothing says it is. The viewer may read it as a special offer or a mistake. Fix: make the four card images match in kind and tone (all illustrations or all photos), unless window cleaning really is the service to push. If it is, give it a label that says so. Taste. Minor.
2. **The prices are the smallest text (not a checklist line).** "From $89" and the other prices (around y 614) are about 15 px, the same size as the card descriptions. Bold and green set them apart, but they sit at the bottom of each card under a gap. A visitor comparing services has to read each card to the end to find the number they are choosing on. Fix: give the price a little more presence, either one size step up or moved next to the title. Taste. Minor.

**What's working.**
- **The headline clearly leads.** It is a large bold serif against a sans-serif page, so the eye knows where to start, and the intro line underneath is much lighter (smaller, regular weight, grey), which keeps the order clear.
- **The cards have a clear internal order.** Each one runs bold title, then regular body text, then a bold green price. That gives three readable levels using only two sizes, done through weight and color rather than extra sizes, which is the approach *Refactoring UI* recommends.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is every element either exactly aligned with an edge or axis it shares with another, or clearly off it, with no near-misses of a few pixels?** In all four cards, the picture panel is inset about 14 px from the card edge (left edge at x≈70 in card 1, ≈368, ≈666, ≈964), but the title, description and price are inset about 20 px (x≈76, ≈374, ≈672, ≈970). The 6 px step repeats down the left side of every card, just under the picture's left edge, so the text looks as if it was meant to line up with the picture and missed. The cards are the main content, so this is the most visible alignment flaw on the page. Arnheim (*Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance") makes the point that a placement that is almost aligned makes the eye waver and the piece look unfinished. Fix: give the text the same inset as the picture, or move it clearly further in so the difference looks deliberate. Defect (small craft). Weight: minor.
2. **Do all blocks, pictures included, take their edges and the gaps between them from one grid, so column lines and gutters repeat down the page?** Nearly everything sits on one grid: the logo, headline, subhead and card 1 share x=56, the "Book a visit" button and card 4 share x=1224, and the four cards have even 24 px gutters. The nav links (x≈520–874) are the exception. They line up with no column, and their centre (≈697) is about 57 px right of the page centre and of the middle gutter (640). They are centred in the space left between the logo and the button, so the header looks *almost* centred, but not on the axis the cards set up. Müller-Brockmann (*Grid Systems*) says every block should take its edges from the shared columns. Fix: centre the nav on the page axis (640), or align it to a card column, for example starting at card 2's left edge (x=354). Convention. Weight: minor.
3. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** All the content ends with the cards at y≈646. Below that is an empty band of about 154 px (y≈646–800), the bottom fifth of the screen, with nothing in it and no hint of a next section. The page looks top-heavy and unfinished rather than intentionally spacious, as if the content stops short of the fold. Arnheim (*Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance", "Weight") says a heavy area needs a counterweight. This would be fine if the next section or a "how it works" row shows above the fold in the live page. If it doesn't, fix it by moving the hero group down so its space above and below matches, or by bringing the next section's start into view. Taste/convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.** The four cards form one steady row: equal widths, one 24 px gutter, and the titles (y≈502), descriptions (y≈534/555) and prices (y≈614) on the same lines in every column. The prices stay aligned even though the descriptions run to different lengths, so the four services compare at a glance. The 56 px left margin is shared by the logo, headline, subhead and first card, which gives the page one strong edge that the eye follows from the top down.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 10 yes, 3 no (one grid; exactly aligned or clearly off; visual weight balances)

sections.report:
**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries, never between a number and its unit or inside a name?** No. The H1 (about x 56–672, y 115–205) wraps as "Help around the house, on your / schedule". The break splits the phrase "on your schedule" and leaves "schedule" alone on the second line. The reader pauses on "on your…" before the payoff arrives, and the heading's shape looks lopsided: a long first line over one short word. The text column looks capped at about 680 px while the page runs to 1224 px, so the break comes from the box width rather than a choice. Fix: break after "house," so the two lines are "Help around the house, / on your schedule", or widen the heading box so it sits on one line. Use a manual or balanced break (for example `text-wrap: balance`), not a narrower box. Taste/common sense: the catalog entry's source for heading breaks is unverified. Weight: minor.
2. **Outside the checklist, copy (prices):** "From $89", "From $189", "From $24" and "From $65" at y ≈ 614 give a price with no unit. The viewer can't tell whether $24 for laundry is per bag, per load or per week, or whether $65 for garden care is per visit or per month. These are the numbers a customer later holds the business to, so reading them two ways is a defect: someone who expects $24 per week and gets billed per load will feel misled. Fix: add the unit, for example "From $24 per bag" or "From $65 per visit". Defect. Weight: minor, and the director may move it to another section.

**What's working.**
- The type plan is clean and holds together. A bold serif carries the wordmark and the H1, and a single sans covers the navigation, subtitle, card titles, body text and prices. The sizes step clearly: H1 at about 40 px, card titles at about 19 px, body at about 15 px, and bold green for the price. Each size has one obvious job, and no two faces nearly match.
- The card copy is short and concrete, and it says what happens: "We collect on Monday and bring it back folded on Wednesday." That gives a who, what and when without the viewer filling gaps. Every description breaks cleanly over two lines with no runts.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (headings break at phrase boundaries)

Every color line on this page passed, so I have no findings in this section. The **Color** report is below.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

Card 1's photo (about x 70–316, y 293–473) is the darkest, brownest block on the page, with oxblood and wood tones that appear nowhere else. It pulls the eye ahead of the other three cards. Under this checklist the palette count leaves out photos and illustrations, so it isn't a color finding. It's a mismatch between the photo and the illustrations, and belongs in the Pictures section.

**What's working.**
- **A tight palette with clear jobs.** Everything outside the pictures uses slate, cream and white, plus one teal. Dark slate does the headline, the wordmark and the "Book a visit" button. Teal appears only on the four "From $…" prices, so the colors look planned rather than picked one at a time (Refactoring UI, "Define your shades").
- **Warm accents on cool panels.** The coral basket, orange pot and mustard dots sit on pale mint panels, so warm shapes come forward and the panels drop back (Itten, warm and cool contrast). Strong color covers only a small share of the area, mostly inside the illustration panels. Most of the page stays cream and white, and the light-to-dark range would still show the structure in grayscale.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Pictures: applies. There are four card images (one photo, three flat illustrations) and a text wordmark.

**Findings**
1. **Do the pictures share one rendering style and one level of detail?** No.
   - **Where:** The "Window cleaning" card (photo at about x 70–316, y 293–473) is a detailed, dark, warm-toned interior photograph: a wood-panelled lounge with leaded bay windows and leather sofas. The other three cards (about x 368–1210, same rows) are simple flat vector drawings (basket, T-shirt, potted plant) on a pale mint tile, using one teal/coral/yellow palette.
   - **What the viewer gets:** The four cards are built to be equal, parallel choices, but the photo is by far the heaviest, darkest and busiest thing in the row, so the eye goes to it first and stays there. That makes window cleaning look like the featured or default service, which nothing else on the page says. The row also stops reading as one family and looks put together from different sources. Most likely a placeholder or stock photo was dropped in where an illustration belonged.
   - **The photo's content:** It works against the card. It shows an ornate hotel- or club-style lounge with no cleaning, no person and no spotless glass, so it doesn't say "streak-free windows". Its upscale-institutional mood also clashes with the friendly flat style of the rest of the page.
   - **Why:** Common sense. Images shown side by side as one set read as one family. Apple HIG, "Icons", asks for a consistent level of detail across a set.
   - **Fix:** Choose one rendering style for the set and replace the image that differs. Here that means a flat illustration for window cleaning (a window with a squeegee, on the same mint tile and palette). Mix styles only if a rule covers the whole design, for example all four as photos with one shared grade and crop.
   - **Type:** Defect (it unbalances a set of equal choices and misdirects the eye). **Weight:** major.

**What's working.**
- **The three illustrations hold together as a system.** They share a flat fill style, a three-colour palette taken from the brand teal plus coral and yellow, the same mint tile, the same centred, front-on viewpoint, and the same scatter of small dots and circles. Each one reads at a glance as its service. Keep this as the template the odd card is brought into line with.
- **The wordmark is well handled.** "Fernway Home Care" is a plain serif wordmark in the brand's dark teal, with generous clear space in the header. It stays legible small and works in one colour.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 11 yes, 1 no (one rendering style and one level of detail), 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes): Interface**

Bash was refused, so I couldn't run the crop and entries scripts. The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image.

1. One primary button: yes. "Book a visit" is the only filled button, and the nav links are plain text.
2. Controls look like what they do: no. The four service cards could be links or could just be information. There's no "Book", "See details" or arrow, and the only cue is a faint shadow. The nav links are fine for a header.
3. Non-text contrast at 3:1: no, if the cards are controls. Their white edge on the cream page looks far below 3:1. If the cards are only content, this is yes.
4. States shown: yes (none shown).
5. Focus indicator: unsure (can't tell from a still).
6. Focus left uncovered: unsure.
7. Main content uncovered: yes.
8. Target size: yes. The button looks about 121×43 and the nav links look 24 px or taller with wide gaps.
9. Phone layout: yes (doesn't apply).
10. Where the user is: no. No nav item shows the current page, and "Services" is presumably what this page is.
11. Way out: yes (no dialog).
12. Inputs allow only valid values: yes (no inputs).
13. Destructive actions set apart: yes (none).
14. Nothing to remember from another screen: yes.
15. Rare options behind a control: yes.
16. Fields labelled: yes (no fields).
17. Control next to what it changes: no. The subhead says "Pick a service, choose a day", but you pick a service from the cards, which have no control, while the only action sits in the top-right corner, apart from the services.
18. Form in one column: yes (no form).
19. Required fields marked: yes (no fields).
20. Errors stated in words: yes (none).
21. Errors say how to fix them: yes (none).
22. Empty state says what to do: yes (none).
23. Help near the step: yes.
24. Shortcuts: yes. It's a four-item marketing page.
25. Puts the next step in front of the user: no. After reading a card, the next step is to book that service, and nothing on the card lets you. The empty band at y≈650–800 is where a next step would go.
26. Follows platform conventions: yes.
27. Audience's own words: yes.
28. Link purpose clear: yes.
29. Instructions name the control: no. "Pick a service, choose a day" describes steps but doesn't point to anything you can pick or choose on this screen.
30. Grouping shows how parts relate: yes.
31. Consistent across screens: yes (one screen).
32. Fits the width: yes.
33. Honest choices: yes.

---

**Section.** Interface: applies (a header nav, one button and four service cards that may be clickable).

**Findings**
1. **"Does every control look like what it does…?"** combined with **"Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them…?"** and **"Does each control sit next to the thing it changes?"**
   - **Where:** the four service cards (x≈56–1224, y≈279–646).
   - **What the viewer experiences:** they're told to "Pick a service", but no card shows a way to pick it. There's no button, no "Book window cleaning →" and no arrow. A white card with a faint shadow might be a link or might not. Someone who has chosen "Deep cleaning · From $189" has to work out that they should click the card or travel up to "Book a visit" in the top right (x≈1103–1224, y≈12–55). That button doesn't know which service they chose.
   - **Why:** clickable things need a signifier (Norman, *The Design of Everyday Things*: signifiers and natural mapping), and buttons and links must look clickable (Nielsen Norman Group). Tognazzini's "anticipation" principle backs the next-step point, but it's off the approved list, so that part is common sense here.
   - **Fix direction:** give each card a visible action tied to its service, such as a text link or secondary button like "Book window cleaning" or "Choose", placed under the price. Or make the whole card an obvious link with an arrow and a hover state. The header "Book a visit" stays the one primary button.
   - **Kind and weight:** defect, major. The page's whole job is to get someone from picking a service to booking.
2. **"Does an instruction name the control it means…?"**
   - **Where:** the subhead at y≈229.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** "Pick a service, choose a day" describes a flow the screen doesn't show. There's no day picker, and there's no pick control on the cards, so the viewer looks for something to pick and finds nothing.
   - **Why:** common sense. The words promise an interaction the interface doesn't offer.
   - **Fix direction:** add the controls the line describes (see finding 1), or reword the line around what this screen actually lets you do.
   - **Kind and weight:** defect, minor. It has the same root as finding 1.
3. **"Does the screen show where the user is…?"**
   - **Where:** header nav (x≈520–874, y≈33).
   - **What the viewer experiences:** "Services", "Pricing", "Service areas" and "Contact" all look the same, so nothing shows which page this is, although the content is the services list.
   - **Why:** Nielsen heuristic 1, visibility of system status.
   - **Fix direction:** mark the current nav item with weight, colour or an underline.
   - **Kind and weight:** convention, minor. On a short marketing site the cost is small.
4. **"Do input borders, control edges, and meaningful icons reach 3:1 contrast…?"**
   - **Where:** the card edges, white on cream (#F9F6EF-ish).
   - **What the viewer experiences:** the edge of each card is held up only by a soft shadow. If the cards are the click targets, their limits are hard to see, especially for people with low vision.
   - **Why:** WCAG 1.4.11, non-text contrast. This applies only if the cards themselves are the controls.
   - **Fix direction:** if the cards stay the click targets, give them a visible border or a stronger edge. If a button inside each card takes over the action (finding 1), this stops mattering.
   - **Kind and weight:** convention, minor.

**What's working.**
- There's exactly one filled, high-contrast button, "Book a visit", and the nav is plain text, so the primary action can't be mistaken. Keep that when adding per-card actions by making those secondary (text links or outlined buttons).
- The header follows the expected pattern: logo on the left, nav in the middle, action on the right. It needs no learning, and its targets look comfortably large.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the cards are clickable at all, and whether they have hover or focus states. Check in a live browser, because finding 1 depends on it.
- Focus indicators on the nav links and the button.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 27 yes, 4 no (one way to act per control: controls look like what they do / control next to what it changes / next step in front of the user; instructions name the control; shows where the user is; non-text contrast of card edges), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not obscured).
